\begin{abstract}
Compound sparsity---simultaneously pruning attention heads and evicting KV cache entries---is essential for efficient LLM inference but produces super-additive quality degradation whose structure is poorly understood.
Prior work treats compound interaction magnitude as approximately constant across the generation process.
We show that this assumption is wrong: compound sparsity severity is an emergent phase-strategy interaction that varies by over an order of magnitude across reasoning phases.

We evaluate compound sparsity on three models---DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (both Qwen2ForCausalLM), and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B (LlamaForCausalLM)---spanning two architectures, using 50 MATH-500 problems, measuring the Interaction Index---a super-additivity metric---across quantile-segmented reasoning phases at sparsity levels $s \in \{0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30\}$.
Under importance-based KV cache eviction, the median Interaction Index difference between low-sparsity and high-sparsity reasoning phases increases monotonically from $0.39$ at $s{=}0.15$ to $14.59$ at $s{=}0.30$, with paired Cohen's $d_z$ growing from $0.44$ (small) to $0.80$ (large); Bonferroni-corrected permutation tests yield $p < 0.005$ at all four sparsity levels.
Random eviction produces no significant phase modulation in 7/8 conditions; the single exception (Qwen $s{=}0.30$, $p{=}0.012$) shows negligible median difference ($\widetilde{\Delta} = \placeholder{}$), confirming that the severity gradient is strategy-specific, not an inherent property of compound sparsity.
At $s{=}0.25$, a crossover emerges: importance-based eviction outperforms random in high-sparsity phases ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}} = 0.032$ vs.\ $0.818$) yet underperforms in low-sparsity phases ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}} = 7.196$ vs.\ $1.363$)---a qualitative reversal in strategy ranking.
The pattern replicates on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct at $s \geq 0.20$ ($d_z \geq 0.55$; Spearman $\rho = 1.0$; gradient permutation $p = 0.043$) and on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B (LlamaForCausalLM), where monotonically increasing median paired differences ($\widetilde{\Delta}$: $0.020 \to 0.356$; $s{=}0.30$ Wilcoxon $p_{\text{Bonf}}{=}0.029$) provide mixed but directionally consistent evidence for cross-architecture generalization, though at ${\sim}$1/40 the absolute magnitude and with substantially weaker interaction than in Qwen2-based architectures. % exp_id: c3_llama

We propose entropy-discrimination collapse as an explanatory mechanism: head pruning flattens cumulative importance scores in phases where attention is already broadly distributed, degrading the discriminative power of importance-based eviction in a phase-dependent manner.
These findings challenge the phase-invariance assumption in compound sparsity deployment and motivate phase-aware compression budgets for reasoning models.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Long-context language models place acute pressure on the key--value (KV) cache, which grows linearly with sequence length \cite{kwon-sosp2023, pope-mlsys2023}.
Two complementary responses---\emph{attention head pruning} \cite{voita-acl2019, michel-neurips2019} and \emph{KV cache eviction} \cite{snapkv-neurips2024, adakv-neurips2025}---can be deployed simultaneously as \emph{compound sparsity}, but the resulting quality degradation is often super-additive \cite{spark-aaai2026, slim-icml2025}. Recent evaluations confirm that reasoning capabilities degrade disproportionately under compound compression \cite{unicomp-2026}, and that per-dimension safe zones intersect to form a smaller joint safe region \cite{phase-transition-compression-2026}.

Prior work treats compound interaction magnitude as roughly constant across generation \cite{spark-aaai2026, unicomp-2026}, despite evidence that pruning sensitivity depends on representational phase \cite{decision-repr-transition-2026} and that no single sparse attention strategy dominates across generation stages \cite{sparse-frontier-2025}.
This assumption is problematic for reasoning models, whose generations alternate between broadly distributed attention (exploratory reasoning) and sharply concentrated attention (structured computation) \cite{thinkv-iclr2026}.
Phase-aware methods like ThinKV \cite{thinkv-iclr2026} apply different KV strategies per phase but without considering compound interaction, while importance-based eviction itself faces challenges from greedy bias \cite{greedy-bias-kvcache-2026}, deferred importance \cite{retentivekv-2026}, and temporal dynamics in long generations \cite{lethe-aaai2026}. These methods each optimize a single pruning axis; we characterize the interaction when multiple mechanisms are composed.
If compound severity varies across these phases, a uniform sparsity budget may be safe in one phase yet destructive in another.

We show that compound sparsity severity is strongly modulated by reasoning phase and eviction strategy.
Under importance-based KV cache eviction, the Interaction Index---a measure of super-additive degradation---concentrates in low-sparsity phases and is largely absent in high-sparsity phases.
On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, the median phase difference rises from $0.39$ at $s{=}0.15$ to $14.59$ at $s{=}0.30$ ($d_z$: $0.44 \to 0.80$; Bonferroni-corrected $p < 0.005$ at all levels).
The pattern replicates at $s \geq 0.20$ on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ($d_z \geq 0.55$) and partially extends to a distinct architecture (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, LlamaForCausalLM) with a qualitatively consistent but substantially weaker trend at $\sim$1/40 the magnitude.
Critically, random eviction produces no such gradient (7/8 conditions non-significant), confirming the gradient is an emergent phase-strategy interaction.

We propose \emph{entropy-discrimination collapse} as a mechanism: head pruning flattens cumulative importance scores in phases where attention is broadly distributed, degrading the discriminative power of importance-based eviction in a phase-dependent manner.
Random eviction is immune because its decisions are independent of attention patterns.
Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item We identify a \textbf{phase--strategy interaction}: importance-based eviction exhibits a severity gradient across reasoning phases that is absent under random eviction (\S\ref{sec:results}).
    \item We show this gradient \textbf{increases monotonically with sparsity} and replicates across three models spanning two architectures (\S\ref{sec:results}).
    \item We propose \textbf{entropy-discrimination collapse} as a mechanistic explanation (\S\ref{sec:analysis}).
\end{enumerate}

1	\section{Analysis: Entropy-Discrimination Collapse}
2	\label{sec:analysis}
3	
4	We propose \emph{discrimination collapse} as the primary mechanism driving the phase-strategy interaction. Head pruning reduces the number of heads contributing to cumulative importance scores, flattening the score distribution: the Gini coefficient decreases by $0.030$--$0.081$ (DeepSeek) and $0.010$--$0.020$ (Qwen) across all sparsity levels, with consistent negative deltas in all 16 conditions (Appendix~\ref{app:analysis}, Table~\ref{tab:discrimination-metrics-full}). When importance scores lose discriminability, thresholding degenerates into noise-sensitive selection---functionally approaching biased random eviction. This effect is phase-dependent: in low-sparsity phases, attention is already broadly distributed, so pruning-induced flattening has maximum impact; in high-sparsity phases, concentration is preserved. Random eviction is immune because its decisions are independent of score quality, explaining $G \approx 1$. % exp_id: c4_entropy_deepseek, c4_entropy_qwen
5	
6	Beyond discrimination collapse, head pruning redistributes the attention entropy of surviving heads. For DeepSeek, the entropy delta is consistently negative ($\Delta\mathcal{H} \in [-0.047, -0.040]$), indicating that importance-based pruning systematically selects heads whose removal concentrates attention in survivors. For Qwen, the pattern partially replicates at $s \leq 0.20$ but reverses at $s{=}0.25$ ($\Delta\mathcal{H} = +0.045$), suggesting model-specific head specialization patterns (Appendix~\ref{app:analysis}, Table~\ref{tab:entropy-deltas}). We characterize discrimination collapse as the robust, model-independent driver, with entropy redistribution as a secondary, model-dependent amplifier. % exp_id: c4_entropy_deepseek, c4_entropy_qwen

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Compound compression.}
Combining multiple compression axes produces non-additive errors.
\cite{spark-aaai2026} report super-additive degradation when combining channel pruning with token eviction; \cite{slim-icml2025} formalize compound error for quantization and sparsity.
\cite{unicomp-2026} evaluate compound compression across 40+ benchmarks, revealing that reasoning capabilities degrade disproportionately.
\cite{phase-transition-compression-2026} characterize independent phase transition points per compression dimension, implying the joint safe region is the intersection of per-dimension safe zones.
GRASPrune~\cite{graspune-acl2026} learns global budget-constrained gates for joint pruning but treats decisions as static across generation.
These works establish compound interaction but share an implicit assumption: interaction magnitude is constant across the generation process.

\paragraph{KV cache eviction.}
Most methods rely on importance scoring whose reliability is increasingly questioned.
Ada-KV~\cite{adakv-neurips2025} introduces per-head adaptive budgets; SnapKV~\cite{snapkv-neurips2024} compresses from a fixed observation window; \cite{defensivekv-iclr2026} show worst-case loss $2.3$--$4.3{\times}$ higher than expected under standard aggregation.
\cite{nacl-acl2024} combine proxy-token and random eviction to counter attention bias.
RetentiveKV~\cite{retentivekv-2026} identifies deferred importance, and \cite{greedy-bias-kvcache-2026} show that single importance metrics exhibit systematic greedy bias.
\cite{hies-2025} independently show that importance-based head discrimination collapses under heavy pruning, further questioning single-metric reliability.
Lethe~\cite{lethe-aaai2026} introduces temporal adaptivity with layer-wise multi-round pruning, and SparK~\cite{spark-aaai2026} extends eviction to the channel dimension with recoverable sparsity.
These methods each optimize a single pruning axis---whether aggregation, metric, temporal, or channel---without characterizing compound interactions when multiple mechanisms are simultaneously active.

\paragraph{Phase-aware inference.}
ThinKV~\cite{thinkv-iclr2026} applies different KV strategies per phase but without compound interaction.
\cite{decision-repr-transition-2026} find pruning sensitivity depends on ``silent'' vs.\ ``decisive'' representation phases.
\cite{doing-more-with-less-2026} show pruning combined with test-time scaling can exceed unpruned baselines; \cite{sparse-frontier-2025} find no universally optimal sparse attention strategy across generation stages.
\cite{physics-kvcache-2026} identify a sharp phase transition in single-axis KV cache compression at high sparsity, characterizing the single-dimension failure mode that our compound analysis extends across multiple axes.
R-KV~\cite{rkv-neurips2025} exploits reasoning-specific redundancy for aggressive cache compression, targeting per-axis optimization rather than characterizing compound degradation.
These works establish phase-dependent compression tolerance along single axes.
Our work bridges this by quantifying how compound severity varies across phases and eviction strategies.

4	This cross-model consistency (Table~\ref{tab:discrimination-metrics-full}) establishes discrimination collapse as a robust consequence of compound sparsity. When importance scores lose discriminative power, thresholding the bottom-$s$ fraction becomes noise-sensitive: small perturbations change which positions cross the eviction boundary. In the limit of perfectly uniform scores, importance-based eviction degenerates into an arbitrary selection functionally equivalent to biased random eviction. The same pattern holds under random eviction (DeepSeek: $-0.031$ to $-0.073$; Qwen: $-0.019$ to $-0.045$), confirming that discrimination collapse is a consequence of head pruning \emph{per se}, not of the eviction strategy. % exp_id: c4_entropy_deepseek, c4_entropy_qwen

7	\section{Extended Discussion}
8	\label{app:extended-discussion}
9	
10	\paragraph{On the predictability of phase-modulated severity.}
11	The compound interaction is not uniformly fragile---it is selectively fragile in a phase-dependent manner ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\text{high}} < 0.06$ at $s \leq 0.30$; at $s = 0.35$, high-phase II rises to $0.105$ in a supplementary experiment, indicating onset of compound interaction even in high-sparsity phases at extreme pruning rates). % exp_id: bf16_importance_s015..s030, bf16_ds_imp_s035; high-phase medians: 0.006, 0.015, 0.032, 0.053; s035 II_high=0.1051

13	\paragraph{Random masking as falsification control.}
14	Random eviction fails 7/8 paired permutation tests across both models; the single exception (Qwen $s{=}0.30$, $p{=}0.012$) exhibits negligible effect size ($\widetilde{\Delta} = \placeholder{}$). The absence of a phase gradient under random masking isolates the amplification as strategy-specific. % exp_id: bf16_ds_rand_s015..s030, bf16_qw_rand_s015..s030
15	
16	\paragraph{Entropy mechanism boundary conditions.}
17	Directly measuring per-head entropy shifts across architecturally distinct models---and identifying what training-time properties determine whether entropy concentrates or disperses under head pruning---would clarify the boundary conditions of the full mechanism.
18

20	\section{Extended Limitations}
21	\label{app:limitations}
22	
23	\paragraph{Model scale.}
24	All experiments are conducted at the 7B parameter scale.
25	Whether the phase-modulated severity patterns persist, amplify, or attenuate at larger scales (e.g., 70B) remains untested.
26	Larger models may exhibit different attention redundancy structures that alter the discrimination collapse dynamics (and the model-dependent entropy component may behave differently at scale).
27	% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "7B is too small to be relevant for production."
28	% REBUTTAL: 7B is the most-deployed scale for on-device and cost-constrained serving—exactly where compound sparsity is needed. The mechanism (entropy-discrimination collapse) is scale-agnostic in principle. Scaling experiments are future work.
29	
30	\paragraph{Architectural scope.}
31	Our two models---DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct---share the Qwen2ForCausalLM architecture.
32	The cross-model replication (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}) establishes that the findings are not artifacts of a single model's weights, though both models share the same Qwen2ForCausalLM architecture.
33	Preliminary cross-architecture validation on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B (LlamaForCausalLM, \S\ref{sec:cross-arch}) shows qualitatively consistent within-importance phase gradients ($d_z \sim 1.0$) but a substantially weaker strategy $\times$ phase interaction than in Qwen2-based architectures; random pruning also exhibits a non-trivial phase gradient on LLaMA, reducing the strategy contrast. This partial confirmation ($s{=}0.30$ Wilcoxon $p_{\text{Bonf}}{=}0.029$; $s \leq 0.25$ non-significant) suggests the qualitative pattern may generalize but quantitative impact is architecture-dependent. Comprehensive cross-architecture validation across more diverse designs (e.g., Mistral, multi-latent attention architectures) and scales remains an important next step.
34	% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "Cross-model ≠ cross-architecture. Both are Qwen2ForCausalLM."
35	% REBUTTAL: We now include cross-architecture validation on LlamaForCausalLM (\S\ref{sec:cross-arch}), which shows a qualitatively consistent but substantially weaker pattern. We use qualified language ("partially supports") rather than claiming full generalization.
36	
37	\paragraph{Task coverage.}
38	We evaluate exclusively on MATH-500, a mathematical reasoning benchmark.
39	Different reasoning tasks---code generation, commonsense reasoning, multi-hop question answering---may induce different phase structures with different sparsity distributions, potentially altering the severity gradient profile.
40	Generalizing the phase-strategy interaction to broader reasoning domains is an important next step.
41	% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "Only MATH-500. How do we know this isn't a math-specific artifact?"
42	% REBUTTAL: The mechanism (entropy-discrimination collapse under head pruning) depends on attention distribution properties, not math-specific features. MATH-500 is a standard benchmark with diverse difficulty. However, different reasoning tasks may induce different phase structures—we state this limitation explicitly rather than overclaiming.
43	
44	\paragraph{Statistical scope.}
45	Bootstrap confidence intervals use $B{=}10{,}000$ resamples (recomputed from initial $B{=}1{,}000$ profiling runs). The paired permutation test yields $n{=}49$ paired problems for DeepSeek (1 excluded) and $n{=}46$ for Qwen (4 excluded). % exp_id: cohens_d_bf16.json, cohens_d_bf16_qwen.json
46	The severity difference distribution is right-skewed (mean/median ratio ${\sim}1.6{:}1$ at $s{=}0.30$), motivating our use of medians and nonparametric tests rather than parametric alternatives. % exp_id: bf16_importance_s030; mean_diff=22.94, median_diff=14.59 (segment-level). Per-problem paired: median_diff=9.9436 at s030
47	All four permutation tests reject $H_0$ after Bonferroni correction ($p_{\text{Bonf}} < 0.005$; Table~\ref{tab:permutation}), with CI lower bounds increasing from $0.19$ to $6.70$---confirming the effect direction at every sparsity level. The permutation CIs at higher sparsity are wider (e.g., $[6.70,\; 16.29]$ at $s{=}0.30$), reflecting genuine variance in per-problem severity amplification. % exp_id: permutation_test_results.json; permutation CIs: s015=[0.19,0.62], s020=[0.69,1.49], s025=[1.66,6.64], s030=[6.70,16.29]
48	
49	A notable exception among the random baselines is the Qwen random condition at $s{=}0.30$, which yields a statistically significant result ($p{=}0.012$) despite negligible effect size ($\widetilde{\Delta} = \placeholder{}$, bootstrap CI spanning zero). % exp_id: qw_rand_s030; B=10000, p=0.012, d=-0.035, negligible
50	This case illustrates that dichotomous significance testing can flag effects of no practical magnitude---reinforcing the importance of reporting effect sizes and confidence intervals alongside $p$-values.
51	
52	\paragraph{Sparsity range.}
53	Our experiments span $s \in \{0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30\}$, a moderate range representative of practical deployment targets.
54	More extreme sparsity ($s > 0.50$) may exhibit qualitatively different interaction dynamics---the sub-exponential growth pattern suggests the severity gradient may plateau, but this remains unverified.
55	Conversely, the lower boundary at which phase-modulated amplification first emerges is not yet characterized.
